 These car brands have the most vehicle recalls historically, based on long-term patterns in U.S. safety data and fleet size
 1 / 12 List slides 10 car brands with the longest recall histories List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated October 20, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 A recall means a safety defect was caught — by the automaker, by a regulator, or by both — before it became a widespread crash pattern. That makes recall counts a poor shortcut for judging build quality. They are a better window into something else: fleet size, parts shared across models, and the share of the car now run by software that no wrench can fix.
 The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration logs every recall issued in the U.S., assigns it a campaign number, and tracks how many vehicles it covers. Those totals swing hard from year to year. One fuel pump supplier or one airbag inflator design can span half a dozen nameplates and several model years. A single campaign can reach a million vehicles on that basis alone. High-volume manufacturers sit near the top of the recall tables almost by default.
 This list treats the car brands with the most recalls as a long-run pattern rather than a single year's scoreboard. A calendar-year ranking depends almost entirely on which defects happen to surface in those 12 months. Rankings also shift after the fact, because recall campaigns are often expanded later to cover additional model years. The brands here share recognizable traits. They sell in large numbers in the U.S., and they reuse platform and powertrain parts across multiple badges. Their electronic architecture also creates defect categories that barely existed 20 years ago — battery management faults, or a touchscreen freeze that blacks out the backup camera.
 Recall frequency and long-term reliability measure different things. A manufacturer that finds problems early, reports them, and repairs them quickly is doing what the system was designed to require. Several brands on this list carry huge cumulative recall totals alongside strong durability records. Owners of any make can run their vehicle identification number through NHTSA's database to see whether an open repair is waiting. The work is free of charge.
 Ford tops U.S. recall tables because of F-150 scale 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Ford $F has sat at or near the top of U.S. recall tables for more than a decade, and the main reason is arithmetic rather than engineering failure. The company moves enormous volume across a lineup running from the F-150 pickup to the Explorer, Bronco, Mustang, and a fleet-heavy range of commercial vans, and it shares parts and software with Lincoln.
 Scale turns ordinary defects into huge campaigns. The F-150 has been the best-selling vehicle in the U.S. for decades, so a flaw in a single latch, wiring harness, or camera module can reach more than a million trucks.
 Several themes recur in Ford 's recall record. Small-displacement EcoBoost engines, including 1.5-liter units, have drawn actions tied to coolant seeping into the cylinders, which can cause overheating and under-hood fire risk. Ford has also issued repeated campaigns over door latch assemblies, where a broken pawl spring tab could leave a door that looked closed but was not fully secured. Rearview camera displays that go blank or distorted have triggered their own recalls, since a nonfunctioning backup image violates federal visibility requirements.
 Software has widened the surface area. A current Ford carries body control modules, driver assistance sensors, and infotainment systems that interact in ways a purely mechanical vehicle never did, and each of those systems generates its own defect category.
 Ford has publicly framed part of its elevated recall count as a consequence of looking harder and reporting earlier. That approach raises the number of campaigns in the short term while reducing the number of owners driving on an unidentified fault.
 For an owner, a high Ford recall tally says more about the company's production footprint and configuration sprawl than about how well any individual truck or SUV is assembled. Ford builds a vast number of vehicles in a vast number of trims, drivetrains, and markets, each with its own supplier parts and calibration files, and every one of those variables is a place a defect can hide. The useful response is not brand avoidance but checking a vehicle identification number against the federal recall database, which is free and updated continuously.
 Stellantis recalls span Jeep, Ram, Chrysler, and Dodge 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Stellantis $STLA routinely posts some of the highest recall totals of any automaker group selling in the U.S., and the structural reason is parts sharing. Jeep, Ram, Chrysler, and Dodge draw on a common pool of engines, transmissions, and electrical architecture, so a single bad component can trigger simultaneous campaigns covering a Grand Cherokee, a Ram 1500, and a Durango.
 Jeep produced one of the defining software recalls in the industry. In 2015, after security researchers showed that a Jeep Cherokee could be controlled remotely through its Uconnect system, Fiat Chrysler recalled about 1.4 million vehicles to patch the vulnerability. It was the first large U.S. recall driven by a cybersecurity flaw rather than a mechanical failure. Uconnect has since required further fixes for screen freezes that leave the rearview camera image blank — a condition that puts a vehicle out of compliance with the federal backup camera rule even though nothing under the hood has broken.
 Ram trucks add their own recurring categories, including tailgate latch mechanisms that can release unexpectedly and let cargo fall into the road.
 Chrysler's minivans have generated separate actions. One covered Pacifica Hybrid models over a fire risk, with owners told to park away from structures and stop charging until a repair was available.
 Takata airbag inflators sit underneath all of it. Stellantis inherited that campaign from Fiat Chrysler, and it stretches across Chrysler, Dodge, Ram, and Jeep vehicles built over many model years. Those actions keep adding to cumulative totals long after the original defect was identified, because the tally reflects vehicles still waiting for repair.
 Corporate structure adds another layer. Stellantis was created in January 2021 by merging Fiat Chrysler with France's Groupe PSA, leaving engineering teams, supplier relationships, and validation processes spread across continents. A defect found in one market has to be assessed against platforms sold in several others, and four North American brand identities sit on top of the same shared hardware.
 General Motors recalls, from the ignition switch to the Bolt EV 
 Illustration: Quartz
 General Motors $GM sits near the top of U.S. recall tables for a structural reason: Chevrolet, GMC, Buick, and Cadillac share engines, transmissions, electrical architecture, and truck platforms. A single faulty component can span the Silverado, Sierra, Tahoe, Yukon, and Escalade at once.
 The defining action in GM's modern history is the 2014 ignition switch recall, which covered roughly 2.6 million small cars including the Chevrolet Cobalt and the Saturn Ion. A switch could slip out of the run position and cut power to the engine, the power steering, and the airbags. GM paid a $900 million penalty under a deferred prosecution agreement with the Justice Department. It also rebuilt the way internal safety concerns move up the chain — a change that raised its recall count in the following years, because more problems were being surfaced instead of absorbed.
 The Chevrolet Bolt EV shows how battery chemistry changes recall math. Manufacturing defects in LG-supplied cells, a torn anode tab combined with a folded separator, created a fire risk. The remedy eventually reached every Bolt EV built from 2017 through 2022, plus the 2022 Bolt EUV, with battery modules replaced rather than patched by software. LG agreed to reimburse GM for most of the cost.
 GM also worked through years of Takata inflator repairs across its trucks and SUVs, and later recalled vehicles fitted with ARC-built inflators, a separate defect that drew its own NHTSA investigation. Seat belt pretensioner anchorage and rearview camera display faults have triggered additional campaigns on full-size models.
 More of GM's recalls now end with a software update sent over the air instead of a service appointment, particularly for driver-assistance and infotainment faults tied to systems such as Super Cruise. That fix still counts as a formal recall in NHTSA's records. As the Chevrolet Equinox EV and Cadillac Lyriq add volume, high-voltage battery and control-software defects should remain a regular feature of GM's record, since those faults often emerge only after months of real-world charging.
 Tesla's recalls are mostly software fixes delivered over the air 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Tesla $TSLA ranks among the most recalled brands in the U.S., though most of its campaigns are closed out with an over-the-air software update rather than a service appointment. Affected cars download the fix while parked, often overnight, and many owners take no action at all.
 That distinction shapes the totals. A Tesla is defined largely by its code. One correction to a single software build can reach every Model 3, Model Y, Model S and Model X $TWTR running that build, and the same patch can span several model years at once. A defect that would cover a few hundred thousand cars at a traditional automaker can cover a million or more here, because one codebase runs the entire lineup.
 The most prominent case came in December 2023. Tesla recalled more than 2 million vehicles to add stronger driver-attention controls to Autopilot. The action followed an NHTSA investigation into crashes in which Teslas struck stationary emergency vehicles. A separate recall in February 2023 covered Full Self-Driving Beta software and how the system handled intersections and posted speed limits.
 Other campaigns have been narrower but equally software-shaped. Regulators flagged automatic window reversal that could pinch a limb, and a seatbelt warning chime that failed to sound under certain conditions. Another action covered warning-light text on the instrument display judged too small to read at a glance. That fix, issued in February 2024, reached roughly 2.2 million vehicles and amounted to a font change pushed remotely.
 Tesla has objected to the framing. Chief executive Elon Musk has said publicly that "recall" is the wrong word for an over-the-air update. NHTSA's position has not changed. Under U.S. law, a remedy for a safety defect or for a vehicle that fails to meet a federal motor vehicle safety standard is a recall, whatever the delivery method.
 Owners still need to confirm the update installed. A car parked outside Wi-Fi range or left on older software can sit unremedied while the campaign shows as issued.
 Honda's recall totals are dominated by Takata airbag inflators 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Honda $HMC sits near the top of U.S. recall tables largely because of one supplier defect: Takata airbag inflators, which Honda installed in more vehicles than any other automaker. The inflators relied on an ammonium nitrate propellant that could degrade after years of heat and humidity, then burst the metal canister on deployment and send fragments into the cabin.
 Honda was the first manufacturer to recall vehicles over the defect, starting with a limited action in 2008. The campaign then widened repeatedly over the following decade. It eventually covered the Civic, Accord, CR-V, Pilot, and Odyssey, plus Acura models built with the same components. Some of the oldest affected cars, built in the early 2000s with the inflator design regulators consider most dangerous, carry "do not drive" warnings instead of standard repair notices.
 That single campaign skews Honda 's numbers. NHTSA describes the Takata effort as the largest and most complex safety recall in U.S. history, spanning 19 vehicle manufacturers. Much of the open recall work attached to Honda involves model years that left showrooms 15 or 20 years ago. That keeps cumulative totals high even in stretches when defects on current models are few.
 Honda 's non-Takata recalls have been smaller in scope. The brand recalled vehicles over Denso-supplied fuel pumps whose internal impeller could swell and seize, stalling the engine without warning — a defect that reached several automakers using the same part. Honda has also recalled Accord sedans over a battery sensor that could admit moisture and create a fire risk. Separate campaigns covered SUVs and minivans whose rearview camera displays went blank when the driver shifted into reverse.
 Recall volume and long-term durability measure different things. A recall count records how many vehicles a defect touched, not how often a given Honda fails in service. Owners can look up outstanding repairs through NHTSA using the 17-digit VIN, and Takata inflator replacement remains free regardless of the vehicle's age or mileage.
 Toyota recalls after the 2010 unintended acceleration crisis 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Toyota $TM issues much of its recall volume before anyone is hurt, catching defects through internal testing and warranty-claim analysis. The company rarely waits for a federal investigation to force the matter. That posture traces to 2009 and 2010, when floor mat entrapment and sticking accelerator pedals prompted recalls covering millions of vehicles and hearings in Congress.
 The fallout was costly. Toyota agreed in 2014 to pay $1.2 billion to settle a U.S. Department of Justice investigation into how it had described the defects to regulators and to the public. It was the largest criminal penalty levied on an automaker in the U.S. at that point. The case reset the company's internal threshold for what counts as a reportable problem, and recall totals since have reflected the lower bar.
 Later campaigns cover both mechanical and electronic faults. Toyota was one of several automakers to recall vehicles over low-pressure fuel pumps built by Denso. The defect could stall an engine while driving, and it also reached Honda $HMC and Subaru models. Toyota has recalled vehicles over airbag inflator and sensor faults, including its portion of the industry-wide Takata campaign. In 2024, it called back certain Tundra pickups and Lexus LX SUVs because machining debris left inside the twin-turbo V6 could cause the engine to stall. Hybrids have drawn separate actions: in 2014, Toyota recalled roughly 1.9 million Prius hatchbacks worldwide over software that could shut the hybrid system down while the car was moving.
 Toyota 's manufacturing footprint inflates the vehicle counts. A defect confirmed at a plant in Japan can trigger near-simultaneous recalls across North America, Europe, and Asia, so a single campaign number often covers an unusually wide pool of cars.
 None of this has dented the brand's durability record. Toyota and Lexus routinely finish near the top of Consumer Reports' annual reliability rankings while carrying heavy recall volume. Counting recalls measures how closely a manufacturer watches its fleet, not how well it builds cars.
 Nissan CVT complaints and occupant-sensor airbag recalls 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Nissan's service record in the U.S. turns on one component more than any other: the continuously variable transmission used across the Altima, Rogue, Sentra, and several other high-volume models. Owners reported shuddering, hesitation under acceleration, and outright failure, and the CVT became the defining powertrain issue of Nissan's modern lineup.
 Much of that exposure was handled outside the formal recall system. Nissan extended warranty coverage on CVT-equipped model years and settled class-action claims from owners, because driveability complaints do not automatically clear the federal threshold of an unreasonable risk to safety that triggers a mandatory recall. The distinction matters when comparing brands by raw recall counts, since a defect can generate years of repair claims without ever appearing in a safety campaign.
 Airbag electronics are a separate and more frequent source of Nissan recalls. The brand has issued campaigns covering airbag control units and occupant classification systems — the seat sensors that decide whether the front passenger airbag arms. A sensor reading an adult as a child or an empty seat can leave that airbag suppressed in a crash, and defects of that severity have produced dealer stop-sale orders until replacement software or hardware was available.
 Component sharing extends the reach of any single bad part. Through the Renault-Nissan-Mitsubishi Alliance, Nissan co-develops platforms, engines, and electronic modules with partner automakers, so one supplier fault can surface in vehicles carrying three different badges and no visual resemblance to one another.
 A large portion of Nissan's cumulative recall total still traces to Takata airbag inflators rather than to anything unique to its own engineering. That supplier defect swept in nearly every automaker selling in the U.S., and remediation stretched across years as replacement inflators were manufactured and shipped. Nissan faced owner complaints over long parts waits at the height of the campaign and widened dealer loaner access in North America.
 Owners can check any Nissan against open campaigns using the vehicle identification number, which a dealer or the NHTSA lookup tool will match to warranty extensions and recalls tied to specific model years.
 Hyundai and Kia engine fire recalls and park-outside warnings 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Hyundai and Kia's recall record is built around one category of defect: engine fires. Both brands, which sit under Hyundai Motor Group, have recalled millions of U.S. vehicles over conditions that could let oil ignite in the engine bay, and owners of some affected cars were told to park outdoors and away from buildings until repairs were done.
 That guidance is the clearest marker of how the defect behaved. A park-outside advisory means the hazard does not end when the driver walks away, so the risk sits with a vehicle in a garage or carport overnight.
 The mechanical root of the largest campaigns was the Theta II four-cylinder engine, where bearing wear could seize the connecting rod, damage the block, and release oil onto hot surfaces. Recalled nameplates crossed both badges, including the Hyundai Sonata and Santa Fe Sport and the Kia Optima and Sorento. Separate engine-compartment fire actions reached other models, among them the Kia Soul and Sportage. Shared powertrain architecture is why a single supplier or machining problem spreads across two brands and several assembly plants at once.
 Electrical faults produced a second wave. Both automakers recalled vehicles over antilock braking system control modules that could short and ignite, a component that stays powered with the car switched off, which triggered more park-outside instructions. Seatbelt pretensioners that could rupture when deployed brought additional recalls across several models.
 Theft brought a different kind of exposure. Many Hyundai and Kia models sold in the U.S. through 2021 lacked engine immobilizers as standard equipment, and a bypass method circulated on social media drove thefts sharply higher. The companies faced class-action litigation and lawsuits from city governments, and responded with free anti-theft software and steering wheel locks rather than a federal safety recall — a distinction that drew criticism from owners and municipalities.
 Hyundai Motor Group's U.S. fleet expanded quickly over the past 15 years, and recall exposure grew with it. The group also extended powertrain warranty coverage on vehicles with the affected engines, a remedy separate from the recall repairs themselves.
 BMW recalls center on the N63 V8 and fire risk 
 Illustration: Quartz
 BMW's recall record skews toward powertrain and electrical fire risk rather than minor convenience defects, which keeps the brand under regulatory attention even though its U.S. sales volume is a fraction of Ford $F 's or General Motors $GM '. The largest single driver has been the N63 twin-turbo V8 fitted to 5 Series, 7 Series and X5 models, an engine tied to heavy oil consumption and heat-related wear in the engine bay.
 BMW addressed the N63 through a customer care package and extended coverage that reached beyond standard warranty terms once the scope of the problem became clear. The design placed the turbochargers inside the V of the block, which sharpened throttle response and saved space but trapped heat in a confined area, punishing seals, hoses and injectors over time.
 Battery cable corrosion accounts for another long-running set of safety campaigns. A degraded positive cable connection can short, overheat and ignite nearby material, and because the same cable design carried across several model lines for years, one campaign could sweep up many nameplates and model years at once.
 BMW was also part of the Takata airbag inflator recall that touched nearly every automaker selling in the U.S. Electric water pump failures on four-cylinder and inline-six engines built in the 2010s became a familiar durability complaint, though those were generally handled as warranty and goodwill repairs rather than federal safety campaigns.
 Raw vehicle counts stay lower for BMW than for mass-market rivals for an unglamorous reason: fewer cars on American roads means fewer cars inside any given campaign. Severity is what sets the record apart. Fire risk and loss of motive power show up more often in BMW notices than screen glitches or labeling errors.
 Remedies almost always require a dealer visit. Corroded cables, cracked seals and overheating components cannot be patched remotely, so BMW owners face a service appointment rather than an overnight update. Mini and Rolls-Royce sit under the same corporate parent, BMW Group, and their campaigns are filed separately even when the underlying part is shared.
 Volkswagen's recall record after the 2015 diesel emissions scandal 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Volkswagen's recall record is shaped less by raw vehicle totals than by the 2015 diesel emissions scandal, in which the company admitted fitting defeat-device software to roughly 11 million diesel vehicles worldwide, including Jetta, Golf, and Passat models sold in the U.S. The case was resolved through criminal penalties and civil settlements exceeding $20 billion.
 That episode sits outside the usual recall framework. Emissions enforcement in the U.S. runs through the Environmental Protection Agency and the California Air Resources Board rather than NHTSA, so the diesel fix campaigns and buybacks were not safety recalls in the regulatory sense. The case still reset how regulators in the U.S. and Europe treat vehicle software as a possible source of deliberate, rather than accidental, non-compliance. Related diesel engines also turned up in Audi models built on shared Volkswagen Group architecture, which widened the scope of the response well beyond the Volkswagen badge.
 Safety recall activity since then reflects a company managing two separate engineering problems at the same time. On the combustion side, campaigns have covered fuel pump failures that can cause an engine to stall and exterior lighting wiring that can short. On the electric side, the ID.4 has drawn recalls tied to instrument cluster software that could leave a driver without a speed readout, and to the high-voltage battery disconnect system.
 The split matters for owners. Volkswagen's gasoline lineup collects the mechanical and electrical defects common across the industry, while its newer electric models generate software-first problems that tend to surface in daily use rather than during validation. Early-generation EV software has been a weak point for the brand, and some corrections have required a dealer visit instead of arriving over the air.
 Volkswagen rebuilt its emissions testing oversight and internal engineering sign-off process after the scandal. Anyone checking a Volkswagen vehicle identification number for open campaigns should look closely at bulletins covering the electric lineup, where software-related fixes have been most frequent.
